description: DharmaNet structured knowledge base of selected Bhagavad Gita verses and Mahabharata episodes used by the Dharma-inspired reasoning layer.
attribution_note: All 'paraphrase' fields are short paraphrases written for this project, not translations or quotations. Bhagavad Gita references use the standard chapter.verse numbering (18 chapters, ~700 verses). Mahabharata episodes are cited at parva (book) level only, because verse numbering differs between the BORI Critical Edition and vulgate recensions. Readers should consult a scholarly translation (e.g., the public-domain K. M. Ganguli Mahabharata translation, 1883-1896) for primary text. Every entry is marked needs_scholarly_review until checked by a qualified scholar.

entries.paraphrase: Overcome by pity and confused about what his duty requires, Arjuna asks Krishna to tell him clearly what is better, and places himself as a student.
entries.interpretation: Genuine moral confusion is treated as the legitimate starting point of ethical inquiry rather than a failure; seeking counsel is appropriate when duties conflict.
alternative_interpretations: Some commentators read Arjuna's confusion primarily as attachment to kin disguised as compassion, rather than as a genuine dilemma.
limitations: Context is a battlefield crisis involving kin; the analogy to everyday dilemmas is interpretive.

entries.paraphrase: Considering his own duty as a warrior, Arjuna should not waver; for one in that role, nothing is better than a fight for what is right.
entries.interpretation: DharmaNet reads svadharma as the responsibilities attached to one's role and commitments (professional, familial, civic): wavering from them because of discomfort is ethically significant.
alternative_interpretations: Traditional readings tie svadharma to varna (social class); DharmaNet explicitly does not adopt a birth-based reading.
Some modern readers interpret svadharma as one's authentic nature or calling rather than an assigned role.
limitations: The verse concerns a warrior in war; it does not license violence or harm in other contexts.
Birth-based (caste) readings of duty are rejected by this system as discriminatory.

entries.paraphrase: If Arjuna declines this righteous struggle, he gives up his own duty and his honour and incurs fault.
entries.interpretation: Avoiding a responsibility is itself a morally weighty act; inaction does not leave one blameless when one's role calls for action.
alternative_interpretations: Can be read as an appeal to reputation rather than to principle; commentators differ on how much weight to give the honour argument.
limitations: Context of a war framed as just; transferring the argument assumes the cause in question is legitimate.

entries.paraphrase: Treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as equal, one should engage in the task; acting so, one incurs no fault.
entries.interpretation: A decision should not be driven by fear of personal loss or hope of personal gain; even-mindedness supports clearer judgment.
alternative_interpretations: Critics note equanimity about outcomes can be misused to dismiss harms to others; DharmaNet applies it to the decision-maker's own gains and losses only.
limitations: Does not mean consequences for others are irrelevant.

entries.concept: Nishkama karma (action without attachment to its fruits)
entries.paraphrase: One's claim is to the action itself, never to its results; do not let results be the motive, and do not cling to inaction either.
entries.interpretation: Choose the action that is right to do rather than the one that maximises personal reward; the verse also warns against using uncertainty about results as an excuse for inaction.
alternative_interpretations: Some argue this is compatible with caring about consequences for others and only rejects selfish attachment; others read it as broadly de-emphasising outcomes, which sits in tension with consequentialism.
limitations: Readings that ignore consequences entirely conflict with harm-prevention concerns; DharmaNet treats it as a check on self-interest.

entries.paraphrase: Dwelling on objects breeds attachment; attachment breeds desire, desire breeds anger, anger breeds delusion, and delusion destroys the capacity for sound judgment.
entries.interpretation: Decisions made in anger or driven by strong personal desire are prone to error; cooling-off and reflection protect judgment.
alternative_interpretations: Often read psychologically (a causal chain of emotion) and also spiritually (bondage to the senses).
limitations: Not a claim that emotions are irrelevant to ethics; care ethics treats emotion as morally informative.

entries.paraphrase: Perform your required work, for action is better than inaction; even maintaining one's life is impossible without acting.
entries.interpretation: Withdrawing from a responsibility is not a neutral option; there is a presumption in favour of responsible engagement.
alternative_interpretations: Some read 'required work' narrowly as ritual or scriptural duty; DharmaNet reads it as role-appropriate responsible action.
limitations: Does not say any action is better than careful waiting; deliberate information-gathering is itself action.

entries.concept: Doing what should be done, without attachment
entries.paraphrase: Therefore, without attachment, always carry out the work that ought to be done; acting without attachment one reaches the highest.
entries.interpretation: Reinforces acting from responsibility rather than personal stake.
alternative_interpretations: Read by some as primarily soteriological (about liberation) rather than ethical guidance.
limitations: Does not specify what 'ought to be done' in a given case; that judgment remains with the human.

entries.concept: Lokasangraha (welfare and cohesion of the world)
entries.paraphrase: King Janaka and others reached fulfilment through action; you too should act with a view to holding the world together for the common good.
entries.interpretation: Action should take into account its effect on the wider community and social order, not just the immediate parties.
alternative_interpretations: Conservative readings take 'holding the world together' to mean preserving existing social order; reformist readings take it to mean the welfare of all.
limitations: 'Social order' readings can be used to justify suppressing dissent; DharmaNet uses the welfare reading and flags this tension.

entries.concept: Leaders set the example others follow
entries.paraphrase: Whatever a prominent person does, others imitate; the standard they set is the one people follow.
entries.interpretation: Choices by people in positions of influence create precedents; this raises the stakes of leaders' conduct.
limitations: Applies most clearly when the decision-maker has visible influence.

entries.paraphrase: Better to carry out one's own duty, even imperfectly, than another's duty well; following another's path is fraught with danger.
entries.interpretation: Responsibility is anchored in one's own role; one should neither shirk it nor usurp roles that belong to others (e.g., due process belongs to proper authorities).
alternative_interpretations: Historically linked to varna-based occupation; modern interpreters often read it as authenticity or professional integrity.
limitations: Birth-based readings are rejected by DharmaNet.
Can be misused to discourage people from stepping outside narrow roles to prevent harm.

entries.paraphrase: One must understand what action is, what wrong action is, and what inaction is; the way of action is deep and hard to grasp.
entries.interpretation: Ethical judgment is genuinely difficult; humility about one's own analysis is warranted. DharmaNet uses this to justify displaying uncertainty.
limitations: Not a reason to avoid deciding.

entries.paraphrase: One who sees inaction within action and action within inaction is wise among people.
entries.interpretation: Choosing not to act is itself a choice with consequences; staying silent can be a consequential act.
alternative_interpretations: Often read metaphysically (the self does not act) rather than ethically.
limitations: DharmaNet's ethical reading is one of several; the metaphysical reading is arguably primary in commentarial traditions.

entries.paraphrase: The wise look with an equal eye on a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste.
entries.interpretation: Impartiality: the moral worth of those affected should not depend on status; supports fairness and non-discrimination.
alternative_interpretations: Some traditions read equal vision spiritually (the same self in all) without implying social equality; DharmaNet draws the ethical implication of impartial concern.
limitations: The verse's own social context included hierarchy; the egalitarian reading is interpretive.

entries.concept: Atmaupamya (seeing others' joy and suffering as one's own)
entries.paraphrase: The highest practitioner, by comparison with oneself, sees the pleasure and pain of all others as equal to one's own.
entries.interpretation: An empathy principle: weigh the suffering of those affected as you would your own.
limitations: Does not resolve conflicts between different people's suffering.

entries.concept: Friendliness and compassion toward all beings
entries.paraphrase: Dear is the one who bears no hatred toward any being, who is friendly and compassionate, free of possessiveness and ego.
entries.interpretation: Even when acting firmly (e.g., reporting wrongdoing), one should act without hatred and with compassion toward those affected, including wrongdoers.
limitations: Describes a character ideal rather than a decision rule.

entries.concept: Daivi sampad (qualities that support right conduct)
entries.sanskrit_term: daivi sampad: abhaya, satya, ahimsa, daya
entries.paraphrase: Among the qualities of those inclined to the good are fearlessness, truthfulness, non-violence, freedom from anger, compassion toward beings and forgiveness.
entries.interpretation: Truthfulness, non-harm, courage and compassion are treated together as marks of good character; an action that requires sacrificing several of them is suspect.
limitations: A list of virtues does not rank them when they conflict.

entries.paraphrase: Disciplined speech is speech that causes no needless distress and is truthful, pleasant and beneficial.
entries.interpretation: How a truth is communicated matters: disclosure should be honest but delivered in a way that minimises needless harm.
alternative_interpretations: Some read the conditions as jointly required (so a painful truth might be withheld); DharmaNet reads truthfulness as non-negotiable and the other conditions as governing manner.
limitations: Interpretations differ on whether a harmful truth may be withheld.

entries.paraphrase: Action begun out of delusion, without regard to consequences, loss, harm to others or one's own capacity, is called tamasic.
entries.interpretation: Reckless action that ignores consequences and harm to others is criticised; this is a point where the Gita explicitly attends to consequences.
limitations: Classifies action types; does not by itself tell which concrete option is reckless.

entries.paraphrase: Clear understanding knows when to act and when to refrain, what should and should not be done, what to fear and what not to fear.
entries.interpretation: Discernment is itself a virtue: knowing when to gather more information and when to act.
limitations: Describes the quality of judgment; it cannot substitute for the judgment.

entries.paraphrase: Having set out this teaching, Krishna tells Arjuna to reflect on it completely and then act as he chooses.
entries.interpretation: Even the Gita's teacher leaves the final choice to the person who must act. DharmaNet adopts this as its human-authority principle.
alternative_interpretations: Some commentators read the following verses (18.64-66) as Krishna's final, more directive counsel.
limitations: Used here as a design principle, not as a claim about the verse's sole meaning.

entries.citation: Mahabharata, Drona Parva (episode of Drona's death)
entries.paraphrase: To stop Drona, the Pandavas announce that 'Ashvatthama' is dead, meaning an elephant of that name. Yudhishthira, famed for truthfulness, confirms it while muttering the qualification; the tradition records a cost to his standing for this deception.
entries.interpretation: Even a technically true but deliberately misleading statement made for a strategic good is portrayed as a moral compromise with a cost.
alternative_interpretations: Some readings emphasise that the deception was necessary to end a destructive slaughter, presenting it as tragic necessity.
limitations: Details vary between retellings and recensions; cited at parva level only.

entries.concept: Silence of the assembly and the subtlety of dharma
entries.paraphrase: After Yudhishthira stakes and loses Draupadi in the dice game, she asks the assembly whether one who had already lost himself could stake her. The elders, including Bhishma, fail to answer decisively, calling dharma subtle, and do not stop her humiliation.
entries.interpretation: Appeals to complexity can become cover for complicity; the silence of those with authority while a vulnerable person is wronged is portrayed as a grave failure.
alternative_interpretations: Some readings see Bhishma's answer as an honest acknowledgment of a hard legal question rather than evasion.
limitations: Cited at parva level; the episode's details differ across versions.

entries.citation: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Bhishma's vow); consequences unfold through later parvas
entries.paraphrase: Devavrata renounces the throne and vows lifelong celibacy for his father's sake, earning the name Bhishma. His sense of obligation to the Kuru throne later keeps him on the Kaurava side even as he recognises their wrongdoing.
entries.interpretation: Loyalty and promises carry real moral weight, but rigid adherence can make one complicit in injustice; commitments should be weighed against what they come to require.
alternative_interpretations: Others see Bhishma's steadfastness as an exemplary virtue of keeping one's word regardless of cost.
limitations: Interpretive link between the vow and later loyalty is a common but not universal reading.

entries.citation: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Krishna's and Kunti's meetings with Karna)
entries.paraphrase: Before the war, Karna learns he is Kunti's eldest son and could join the Pandavas, but he refuses to abandon Duryodhana, who had stood by him, out of loyalty and gratitude.
entries.interpretation: Personal loyalty and gratitude are genuine obligations, yet they can bind a person to a cause they know to be wrong; the story invites weighing loyalty against justice.
alternative_interpretations: Many readers regard Karna's choice as admirable fidelity; others as a tragic error.
limitations: Cited at parva level; the story is a narrative, not a rule.

entries.citation: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Vidura's counsel to Dhritarashtra)
entries.paraphrase: Vidura repeatedly counsels King Dhritarashtra to act justly toward the Pandavas and restrain Duryodhana; his candid advice is heard but not followed.
entries.interpretation: Advisers have a duty to speak honestly to those in power even when unwelcome; internal escalation is honourable but may not suffice.
alternative_interpretations: Vidura is sometimes criticised for staying within the court rather than taking stronger action.
limitations: Cited at parva level.

entries.citation: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva (Bhishma's instruction to Yudhishthira)
entries.paraphrase: Bhishma, instructing Yudhishthira after the war, distinguishes the norms of ordinary times from those permissible in emergencies and distress.
entries.interpretation: Context matters: emergencies can justify departures from normal procedure, but the burden of justification is on the one claiming an emergency.
alternative_interpretations: Critics warn that emergency reasoning is easily abused to justify wrongdoing.
limitations: Cited at parva level; highly susceptible to misuse as a rationalisation.

entries.concept: Yudhishthira's impartial choice before the Yaksha
entries.paraphrase: Offered the life of one brother, Yudhishthira chooses Nakula, son of Madri, rather than his full brothers, so that each of his father's wives would have a living son.
entries.interpretation: Fairness can require setting aside partiality toward those closest to us; impartiality is valued.
limitations: Cited at parva level.

entries.paraphrase: The Mahabharata repeatedly praises non-harm as among the highest forms of dharma, even as its narrative depicts a war it frames as necessary.
entries.interpretation: Avoiding harm carries great weight, but the epic itself shows that non-harm can conflict with other duties; it is a strong presumption rather than an absolute rule here.
alternative_interpretations: Jain and some Hindu traditions treat ahimsa as near-absolute.
Popular quotations sometimes add a continuation about justified violence that is not reliably attested; DharmaNet does not use it.
limitations: Cited at parva level; the phrase occurs in several places.
